A reworked wireframe and wireflow for this step have been created, incorporating a “not sent yet” banner and draft invite list [4][5].

questions.question: Which onboarding steps are required, and which can be skipped?

seeded.answer:
According to the canonical step numbering, the onboarding flow includes six steps: Signup, Basics, Connect calendar, Invite your team, Preferences, and Review & finish [1]. Step 3, “Connect calendar”, is a required step, as 2 of 3 participants in initial usability sessions attempted to skip it, despite it being mandatory [2][3]. Similarly, Step 2 (“Basics”) also has a required indicator, causing one participant to express frustration when they initially tried to skip it [4].

Step 3 previously caused confusion, with participants attempting to exit the step by clicking the step label itself, indicating they perceived it as optional [5][6]. However, the documentation notes that this step is now clearly marked as required [1]. Step 4 (“Invite your team”) now shows a draft/not-sent state, addressing participant concerns about immediate sending of invitations [1][7]. The documentation does not specify whether steps 1, 5, or 6 are required or skippable.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the citations in the prior auth drafts?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted to see the specific chart text behind each suggestion, described as “show your work” [1]. This request came from testing in April 2025, where 4 utilization review nurses and a supervisor participated [2][3]. In the November 2025 follow-up testing with the same group of 4 nurses, 3 of 4 participants actively clicked on at least one citation to verify the information, finding it appropriately fast rather than adding friction [4]. The system was updated to provide citations that resolve to specific chart-text spans [5], and this feature was validated as actively used in the November 2025 testing [6]. One supervisor participant stated, “This is what I wanted in April. It shows its work, it got the codes right, and it didn't try to be a hero on the complicated case” [7].

sources.excerpt:

questions.question: How were sound-alike medication names handled?

seeded.answer:
Initially, sound-alike medication names were treated as a monitored issue rather than a launch blocker [1]. The existing system highlighted them as low confidence, but this was considered insufficient [2][1]. A dedicated, visually distinct flag was then tested to see if participants would recognize and react to it differently [2].

In a usability test with 6 physicians and nurse practitioners, 5 out of 6 participants correctly identified the new flag as different from the general low-confidence indicator [3]. However, 2 of the 6 participants reported that the flag made them overtrust medication lines that were not flagged [3][4]. The design of the flag places it inline, immediately after the medication name, and uses a small amber pill-shaped badge [5]. The flag’s copy is “Possible sound-alike medication name — verify before signing” to encourage verification [5]. The placement was chosen after testing showed a 5:1 preference over a right-hand margin badge [5].

sources.excerpt: A distinct sound-alike-medication flag outperforms generic confidence highlighting for this specific error class. The GA-candidate round treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. sources.excerpt:
Placement: inline, immediately after the medication name — tested 5:1 over a right-hand margin badge, since participants didn't want to look away from the text.
Visual treatment: small amber pill-shaped badge, distinct in shape and color from the existing subtle low-confidence underline, so the two signals are never visually conflated.
Copy: short on-hover/on-tap label — "Possible sound-alike medication name — verify before signing" — worded to prompt verification, not to assert an error.

seeded.answer:
Initially, sound-alike medication names were treated as a monitored issue rather than a launch blocker [1]. The existing system highlighted them as low confidence, but this was considered insufficient [2][1]. A dedicated, visually distinct flag was then tested to see if participants would recognize and react to it differently [2].

In a usability test with 6 physicians and nurse practitioners, 5 out of 6 participants correctly identified the new flag as different from the general low-confidence indicator [3]. However, 2 of the 6 participants reported that the flag made them overtrust medication lines that were not flagged [3][4]. The design of the flag places it inline, immediately after the medication name, and uses a small amber pill-shaped badge [5]. The flag’s copy is “Possible sound-alike medication name — verify before signing” to encourage verification [5]. The placement was chosen after testing showed a 5:1 preference over a right-hand margin badge [5].

sources.excerpt: Accuracy: Medication dosage errors dropped from 3/5 sessions (v0.1) to 1/5 (v0.2), driven by fixing outright garbling; the remaining error class is specifically sound-alike medication names, which is now a tracked, monitored issue rather than a blocker.

questions.question: List the onboarding steps in order.

seeded.answer: The onboarding flow consists of six steps [1][2]. Step 1 is Signup, followed by Step 2: Basics, then Step 3: Connect calendar, Step 4: Invite your team, Step 5: Preferences, and finally Step 6: Review & finish [1][2]. Early records sometimes referred to the calendar connection as “step 2” and the invite step as “step 3”, but these refer to the same steps as the canonical numbering [2]. The prototype covers all six steps [3], and the heuristic evaluation also covered the full wizard [4].

questions.question: What is the current session timeout?

seeded.answer: The current session timeout is 10 minutes [1][2][3]. IT Security described this as a fixed policy in February 2026 [1], and this was confirmed by an IT Security stakeholder during a contextual inquiry with 5 participants (Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security) on February 17, 2026, who stated it was not adjustable per-feature [2]. The team is focusing on improving the UI communication during this timeout, not changing the timeout itself [4][5]. Currently, a locked session during active dictation is perceived as data loss, with 4 observed clinicians restarting dictation unnecessarily [3].

sources.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

questions.question: What percentage of clinicians report burnout?

seeded.answer: The September survey of 287 clinicians (Physician, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Registered Nurse) found that documentation burden was the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically, at 52% [1][2]. This was ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1][2]. Additionally, 64% of physician respondents reported regularly completing documentation after clinic hours, averaging 1.2 hours per day [1][2].

questions.question: How aware were staff of the Compass AI initiatives?

seeded.answer: According to a December 2025 survey of 421 staff members, 71% of clinical staff reported awareness of Compass AI initiatives [1]. However, only 34% of non-clinical staff were aware, indicating a significant awareness gap [1][2]. This suggests internal communications have been clinically focused and may need to be broadened if non-clinical rollouts, such as scheduling, proceed [1][2].
